title: Determining what the agreement requires
summary: Interpretation determines the meaning and scope of the parties’ agreement. It asks what their words and conduct mean in the relevant setting, including the evidence the governing law permits the court to consider.
notes:
Begin with the language and the issue in dispute. A disagreement about meaning is different from a claim that an additional agreement should be included. The parol evidence rule addresses the effect of a final written agreement on earlier or contemporaneous terms. Rules about extrinsic evidence address what may be considered in interpreting the words that remain.

Pacific Gas and Trident examine a context-sensitive approach and its consequences. W.W.W. Associates and Greenfield emphasize the written language where it is unambiguous under their approach. Frigaliment and Hurst show the importance of commercial meaning. Nanakuli, Figgie, and Columbia Nitrogen address established practices that may explain or supplement an agreement. These decisions cannot be reduced to a universal instruction either to ignore context or to admit all context.

The case index includes relevant decisions from formation and performance because interpreting a commitment also determines whether a promise exists, how discretion is constrained, and whether conduct amounts to breach.

LRS.title: Interpreting legislation: enacted text and statutory context
LRS.summary: Textualism gives controlling weight to the meaning of the enacted words in their relevant linguistic and legal context.
LRS.notes:
The approach protects the terms on which legislation actually secured enactment and resists substituting unenacted intentions or general policy aspirations. In Katzmann’s account, modern textualism uses context, established terms, ordinary usage, and conventions rather than treating dictionary definitions as invariably decisive. Criticism of legislative history also rests on bicameralism, presentment, and concerns about who speaks for the legislature.

Thomas’s Dolan and Small dissents illustrate disagreements over whether ordinary meaning already supplies a clear answer. Katzmann argues that excluding legislative history can discard useful evidence; textualists argue that using it can empower selective or unrepresentative statements. The existence of these disagreements does not mean every textualist always reaches one result, as Scalia’s vote in Dolan illustrates.

Katzmann’s competing account of legislative purpose

Identify the problem Congress addressed, the means it enacted, and the level of generality at which a claimed purpose operates. Katzmann’s version generally respects unambiguous text and uses reliable context to resolve uncertainty. The Hart-and-Sacks account limits interpretation to meanings the words can bear and recognizes clear-statement rules.

Holy Trinity is the source’s historical example of purpose narrowing broad coverage. Raila tests a proposed reading against the tort statute’s purposes and neighboring provisions. The Murphy litigation shows a disagreement about whether expert-fee reimbursement implements Congress’s intended scheme or exceeds the enacted authorization. A broad policy goal alone does not answer how Congress resolved a particular compromise, and the reading expressly acknowledges difficulty identifying a single purpose.
